framework: AP Seminar (AP Capstone) Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2024)
subject: Seminar (AP Capstone)

outcomes.text: Place a problem or issue in context and identify what makes it complex.
Know that examining others' views raises new questions, and that inquiry starts by narrowing scope, finding the issue's origins and setting it in a larger context.
Pose questions that reflect multiple, divergent or contradictory perspectives.
Know that good research questions account for the complexity of an issue.
Know that inquiry draws on curiosity and imagination to explore complex issues.
Retrieve, question, organise and use what you already know about a topic.
Know that understanding also comes from experience, outside sources, culture and assumptions, not just collecting information.
Know strategies such as brainstorming, concept maps and drafting for organising and connecting ideas.
Know that inquiry can confirm or challenge your existing beliefs and knowledge.
Find and manage information using effective strategies.
Tell secondary sources from primary sources, including self-collected data such as surveys and interviews.
Know that online databases and library catalogues hold secondary and some primary sources.
Use advanced search tools, Boolean logic and keywords to refine a search.

topics.title: EU 1.4 Relevance and credibility of sources

outcomes.text: Judge how relevant and credible a source is for your inquiry.
Know that the scope and purpose of research and source credibility affect how far conclusions can be generalised and trusted.
Know that credible evidence comes from relevant, reliable, current and authoritative sources.
Judge credibility by checking the author's and publisher's credentials, perspective, methods, and peer review.
Identify the information your inquiry needs given its context.
Know that how a problem is framed guides what information and gathering method are needed.
Use suitable reading strategies and read critically for a purpose.
Read closely to find the main idea, tone, assumptions, context, perspective, reasoning and evidence.
Preview and prioritise text by skimming, scanning, rereading and questioning.
Make meaning by annotating, note-taking, highlighting and reading aloud.
Know that perspectives are shared in written, spoken, visual or performance texts and carry the author's tone.
Summarise a text's main idea or aim without faulty generalisation or oversimplification.
Know that a main idea often sits in a thesis, claim or conclusion, or is implied.
Know that artistic works convey perspective and are understood through context, structure, style and aesthetic.

topics.title: EU 2.2 Evidence and lines of reasoning

outcomes.text: Explain and analyse the logic and line of reasoning of an argument.
Know that a line of reasoning is claims justified by evidence.
Know that reasoning is organised by purpose, for example to show causes, define or propose a solution.
Distinguish inductive reasoning from specific cases from deductive reasoning from general facts.
Know that missing the complexities of an argument leads to oversimplification.
Know that strong arguments address others with concession, refutation or rebuttal.
Judge how relevant and credible the evidence for an argument is, in context.
Know that an argument's time, purpose and relation to other arguments inform its interpretation.
Know that writers use qualitative and quantitative evidence of varying validity.
Know that authors choose evidence strategically.
Spot persuasive techniques such as loaded language, authority, qualifiers and fallacies.
Know that evidence can show comparative, causal or correlational relationships, patterns and trends.
Know that credibility drops when authors ignore limits, opposing views or their own biases.
Evaluate whether an argument is valid.
Know that an argument is valid when its reasoning logically supports its conclusion.
Connect an argument to broader issues by examining its implications.
Know that arguments' consequences can be intended or unintended.
Evaluate possible resolutions or solutions an argument raises.
Know that arguments have real-world impact by influencing behaviour.
Identify, compare and interpret multiple perspectives on an issue.
Know that a perspective is shaped by background, assumptions, worldview and outside sources.
Know that perspectives can agree, complement or compete.
Evaluate alternate or competing arguments by their implications and limits.
Recognise arguments that appeal to emotion, values, bias, assumptions or logic.
Remember that your own biases and assumptions affect your judgement of arguments.
Form a well-reasoned argument that accounts for the issue's complexities.
Know that effective arguments use reason and evidence to convey a perspective stated or implied in the thesis or conclusion.
Know that effective arguments are unified by carefully connected claims, reasons and evidence.
Use qualifiers to limit claims and build credibility by avoiding overgeneralisation.
Acknowledge and answer other arguments with concession, refutation or rebuttal.
Know that a line of reasoning is a clear logical path from reasons to conclusion.
Know that reasoning may be deductive (claim then evidence) or inductive (evidence then conclusion).
Organise a line of reasoning by purpose, such as showing causes, evaluating, defining or proposing a solution.
Arrange claims and evidence spatially, chronologically or by importance to convey relationships.
Know that one argument can be organised or supported in several ways depending on audience and context.
Interpret, use and synthesise qualitative and quantitative information from varied sources to support an argument.
Know that evidence comes from print and non-print sources, experts, and fieldwork such as interviews and observations.
Know that compelling evidence is sufficient, accurate, relevant, current and credible.
Choose evidence by context, purpose and audience, for example to cite authority, define, illustrate or qualify.
Know that well-chosen, attributed evidence builds your argument's credibility.
Write insightful commentary that links evidence to claims.
Know that commentary connects evidence to a claim through interpretation, naming patterns, trends or relationships.
Credit knowledge and ideas accurately and ethically with an appropriate citation style.
Know that accurate, ethical attribution enhances your credibility.
Know that plagiarism means presenting others' ideas or words as your own and is avoided by thorough acknowledgement.
Introduce, integrate or embed source material into the text of your argument.
Credit and cite quoted and paraphrased material following a style manual.
Know that disciplines use style guides such as APA, MLA, Chicago and AMA.
Extend an idea, question, process or product to create new understanding.
Know that innovative solutions challenge assumptions, explore alternatives and use reflective skepticism.
Offer resolutions or conclusions based on evidence, considering limits and implications.
Weigh the advantages and disadvantages of options against the goal when proposing a solution.

units.title: Big Idea 5: Team, Transform, and Transmit

outcomes.text: Plan, produce and present a cohesive argument for the audience, context and purpose.
Know the parts of an argument: introduction, thesis, reasons and evidence, counterargument, conclusion and bibliography.
Use transitions so ideas flow logically and smoothly.
Follow conventions of grammar, usage, style and mechanics.
Express tone through word choice, sentence structure and imagery.
Vary sentence structure for emphasis and interest while keeping agreement, modifiers and tense correct.
Use precise words to avoid confusion and wordiness.
Know that spelling and grammar errors undermine credibility.
Communicate through suitable media with effective design.
Use headings, layout, captions and similar elements to help the audience, without overusing them.
Present data graphically with infographics, graphs, tables or models.
Choose media such as essay, poster, talk or documentary to suit context, purpose and audience.
Adapt an argument to its context, purpose and audience.
Adapt arguments by selecting and emphasising information for audience, situation, medium and purpose.
Engage an audience with effective delivery or performance techniques.
Vary volume, tempo, movement, eye contact and energy to emphasise and engage.
Contribute individually to a team's effort towards a shared goal.
Know that sharing your strengths and challenges makes your contribution more effective.
Foster a constructive team climate, resolve conflict and enable everyone's contribution.
Know that teams are built around tasks and that low-risk team activities help performance.
Know that teams do best when they understand their members' diverse backgrounds, talents and skills.
Practise communication, consensus building, conflict resolution and negotiation.
Consider online collaborative tools for teamwork.
Reflect on and revise your own writing, thinking and creative process.
Know that reflection is ongoing and recursive, using journals, self-questioning, drawing or guided contemplation.
Know that learning needs iterative practice: rethinking, revising and rewriting.
Reflect on collaborative experiences.
Reflect on how actions affected the group and individuals, and on whether assumptions helped or hindered the task.
